questions.enonce_markdown:
Discuss the link between Luke and Acts of the Apostles.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles are two volumes of one work. Both are addressed to Theophilus (Luke 1:3; Acts 1:1), and Acts begins by referring to "the first book" in which the author dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach (Acts 1:1). Christian tradition ascribes both books to Luke, the doctor and companion of Paul (Colossians 4:14; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11). The link between them may be seen in authorship, structure, themes and purpose.

**1. Common authorship and style.** The two books share vocabulary, style and good Greek, a similar interest in historical setting (Luke 1:1-4; 3:1-2) and the same dedication. In the later part of Acts the "we" passages suggest that the author was a travelling companion of Paul.

**2. Continuity of the story.** The Gospel ends with the risen Lord's commission and the Ascension (Luke 24:44-53), and Acts begins with the same events retold (Acts 1:1-11). Luke thus forms a bridge: what Jesus *began* to do and teach, the church now continues through the Spirit.

**3. A common plan: from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.** The Gospel moves toward Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), the place of death and resurrection, and the risen Lord says that repentance and forgiveness will be preached to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47). Acts follows this pattern, "in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth" (Acts 1:8), and ends with Paul preaching in Rome.

**4. The Holy Spirit.** The Spirit is active in the Infancy Narratives, at the baptism and in the ministry of Jesus (Luke 1-4); Jesus promises the Spirit (Luke 24:49), and the promise is fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2). The Spirit guides the church as it had guided Jesus.

**5. Parallels between Jesus and his followers.** Peter and Paul heal as Jesus did, for example the lame man at the Beautiful Gate (Acts 3) compared with the paralytic in Luke 5:17-26. Stephen's death echoes the Passion: he commits his spirit and prays for forgiveness of his killers (Acts 7:59-60; compare Luke 23:34, 46). Both Jesus and Paul are tried before governors and kings and declared innocent.

**6. Shared themes.** Both books stress prayer, joy, concern for the poor, the place of women, salvation for Gentiles and Samaritans, and the fulfilment of the Old Testament. The journey motif is also common to both.

**7. A shared purpose.** Both seek to give assurance to Theophilus and other readers about the Christian faith (Luke 1:4) and to show that the church is the legitimate continuation of Israel's story and the instrument of God's saving plan for all peoples.

**Conclusion.** Luke and Acts are best understood as two volumes of one narrative. The Gospel tells of what Jesus did in his earthly life; Acts tells how the risen Lord continues his work through the Spirit and the apostles. Neither can be fully understood without the other.
